newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall again on rate fears, bonds edge higher.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall again on rate fears, bonds edge higher.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed lower on Thursday for the fourth time in five days amid lingering fears of rising U.S. interest rates, while bonds edged higher ahead of Friday's key March employment report.
The dollar fell after the release of strong German economic data and a report from the International Monetary Fund that said the Japanese yen had room to rise.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 39.66 points to end at 6,477.35, standing just above its 1997 start of 6,448.27.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,516 to 894 on active volume of 495 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
A rally in battered technology stocks buoyed the Nasdaq Composite index, which ended 12.76 points higher at 1,213.76.
All eyes were on Friday's report on payrolls, wages and unemployment for March, and the possible impact that the data might have on whether the Fed again raises interest rates.
"It could be a killer if it goes the wrong way," said Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expected the jobless rate to show a 0.1 percent drop to 5.2 percent and non-farm payrolls to rise by 196,000.
The focus also will be on possible upward pressures on wages.

Last week, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than two years in a politically controversial move to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep the economic expansion on track.

If the jobs report shows a more robust-than-expected economy, it will add to growing fears among investors that the Fed will have to further raise interest rates in order to cool the economy, analysts said.
"It appears that the market's already anticipating a number that's going to cause further indigestion," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management.

With Thursday's losses, the Dow has shed more than 400 points since its steep downturn began a week ago. The closely watched gauge of 30 blue-chip stocks has fallen 8.6 percent since its record closing high of 7,085.16 on March 11.
In the bond market, the 30-year bond rose 2/32, or 62.5 cents on a $1,000 bond, leaving its yield unchanged at 7.07 percent.
The dollar fell to 122.59 Japanese yen and 1.6695 German marks in late trading from 123.24 yen and 1.6755 marks late Wednesday.
Pork prices soared after Japan said it was considering cutting a duty on imports of pork due to rising domestic prices.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, the June hog contract closed up the allowable 2-cent a pound daily limit at 82.325 cents and pork bellies for delivery in May closed at 80.175 cents, up 1.875 cents.

At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures closed sharply lower as commodity funds sold off, traders said. Coffee for delivery in May closed 15.45 cents a pound lower at 177.70 cents.
Overseas, London's leading blue-chip FTSE index finished 22.0 points lower at 4,214.6. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average gained 92.01 points to 18,129.31.
